contributing.title: Contributing and testing
contributing.text: Contributing and testing Layout src/ the library, one module per file test/ unit tests, one file per module (dom.test.ts tests dom.ts) test/lib/ the small test runner bin/ esbuild, and scripts to test and check types docs/ this documentation, published to GitHub Pages No Node.js Like the apps made with it, GTD itself needs no Node.js or npm. Everything runs with the files in bin/ , a shell and a browser. Command What it does bin/test.sh Builds the tests with esbuild and runs them in headless Chrome or Chromium bin/test.sh --build Only builds them; open test/index.html in any browser to see the results bin/install-ts.sh Downloads the native TypeScript compiler ( bin/tsgo ) with curl, once bin/tsgo -p . Checks the types of src/ and test/ If your Chrome is not found, point to it: CHROME=/path/to/chrome bin/test.sh . test/index.html is also a visual report: green for passing tests, red for failing ones, with the reason. The test report in the browser: every module with its tests in green GitHub runs the type check and the tests on every push and pull request ( .github/workflows/test.yaml ). Writing a test import { describe, expect, it, mock } from "./lib/test.js" import { setDomEvents } from "../src/dom.js" describe("dom", () => { it("adds listeners", () => { const button = document.createElement("button") const click = mock(() => {}) setDomEvents(button, { click }) button.click() expect(click).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) }) }) Then import the new file in test/index.ts . Helper Use it to expect(x).toBe / toEqual / toContain / toMatch / toBeTruthy / toBeFalsy Check values mock(fn?) Make a function that remembers its calls; check with toHaveBeenCalledTimes / toHaveBeenCalledWith fakeFetch({ path: body }) Answer fetch from memory during the test (404 for other paths) replace(object, key, value) Swap a property, like window.matchMedia , during the test quiet("error" \| "warn") Silence and count console messages during the test afterThis(fn) Clean up after the test, even when it fails Some habits that keep the suite reliable: Network: never call a real server; use fakeFetch . Module state: router.ts and i18n.ts keep state for the whole page. Their tests run in order and build on each other; add new ones at the end. The page: remove what you add to document.body with afterThis . Conventions Every exported function has a JSDoc comment. Compare with the constant first: undefined == value , false == buffer.has(id) . A module imports its siblings with .js ( ./dom.js ), as TypeScript and esbuild expect. A new module gets a test file and a page in docs/5-guides/ or docs/6-reference/ , linked from docs/1-overview.md . Documentation GTD is simple, and its docs should feel the same. Someone who has never used it should have something on screen in minutes. When you write a page: Start with "In 30 seconds" : the smallest example that works, then explain. Show, then tell : code first, then a table or a sentence about it. Write for a junior : short sentences, plain words, explain any term the first time (or link How GTD thinks ). Every example must run as written: imports with .js , await where needed. End with a full example and "Common mistakes" when the module has pitfalls. Link both ways : from docs/1-overview.md to the page, and back with [← All the documentation] . Name files for the menu : a number for the order and readable words ( 3-talking-to-a-server.md ); papiro shows Talking to a server and hides the number. The docs/ folder is published with papiro by .github/workflows/publish-docs.yaml on every push to main . Link pages with relative .md links: they work on GitHub and papiro turns them into site links. GitHub Pages must serve the gh-pages branch: Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages / root . ← All the documentation

core-ideas.title: How GTD thinks 🧠

sections.text: A few words you will see 📖

core-ideas.text: How GTD thinks 🧠 GTD is small on purpose. Six ideas explain how every module behaves. Once you know them, you can guess how most of the library works before reading about it. Idea In one line 1 Everything is the real thing A GTD button is a <button> 2 Nothing to install One builder, no Node.js, no node_modules 3 One file, one job Take the modules you need, leave the rest 4 Functions, not classes Call a function, pass an object, done 5 You draw, GTD doesn't re-draw No magic: you decide what changes on screen 6 Quiet when things are missing Missing pieces never crash your page 1. Everything is the real thing 🧱 GTD is a power drill , not a robot. It makes the job faster, but you are still the one holding the tool, and you can see exactly what it does. It never hides the browser from you. uiComponent returns an HTMLElement , the same object document.createElement gives you. httpGet returns the same Response that fetch gives you. Settings are stored in localStorage . So anything you find on MDN or Stack Overflow still works: const button = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: "Save" }) button.disabled = true // plain DOM button.focus() // plain DOM button.textContent = "Saved" // plain DOM 2. Nothing to install 🎒 Travel light: GTD fits in your backpack. No Node.js, no npm, no node_modules . GTD is a folder of .ts files, and esbuild — one program, one command — turns your app into one .js file. Your project has no dependencies that can break, go out of date or need updating. 3. One file, one job 🧰 Like a toolbox : you take the screwdriver, not the whole box. Each module lives in its own file and does one thing: dom.ts builds elements, router.ts picks pages, http.ts talks to servers. Import only what you use: import { uiComponent } from "./gtd/dom.js" import { httpGet } from "./gtd/http.js" You can even delete the modules you don't need from your copy. 4. Functions, not classes 🍳 Like a recipe : take this, do that . No family tree of objects to learn first. There are no classes to extend and no lifecycle to learn. You call functions and pass plain objects (the few helpers grouped in a class, like Shortcuts , are used the same way, with no new ): uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Hi" }) httpPost({ url: "/api/notes", parameters: { text: "Buy milk" } }) setRoute("/notes", showNotes) 5. You draw, GTD doesn't re-draw 🎨 A whiteboard , not a smart screen: when something changes, you wipe it and draw it again. A bit more work, and never a surprise. GTD does not watch your data. When something changes, you update the element yourself, or draw the page again: let count = 0 const counter = uiComponent({ type: "p", text: "0" }) const button = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: "+1" }) setDomEvents(button, { click: () => { count++ counter.textContent = `${count}` // you decide what changes }, }) This is a bit more typing than in big frameworks, but there is no magic: what you see in your code is exactly what happens on screen. 6. Quiet when things are missing 🤫 Like a good waiter : if the dish you ordered is not available, you get told politely — the restaurant doesn't burn down. GTD prefers doing nothing over crashing your page: Situation What GTD does setDomClasses(element, undefined) Returns the element unchanged getText("bundle", "missing-key") Returns "" getIcon("icons", "missing") Returns undefined A route nobody registered Shows the "not found" view When something does not show up, check the browser console: GTD writes a warning there when it can. A few words you will see 📖 Word Meaning Element A piece of the page, like <h1> or <button> . In code, an HTMLElement . Module A .ts file that exports functions. esbuild The program that turns your .ts files into one .js file for the browser. View A function that draws one page into a container. Route An address, like /user/7 , linked to a view. Signal A named event that several parts of the app can listen to. Bundle A JSON file with the texts of one part of the app, in one language. async / await How JavaScript waits for slow things (network, files) without freezing the page. Most GTD functions that touch the network are async , so put await in front of them. ← All the documentation · Next: The GTD quest →

getting-started.title: Getting started 🚀
getting-started.text: Getting started 🚀 🎯 Goal Your first GTD app in the browser: two pages and a button ⏱️ Time About 5 minutes 🧰 You need A terminal, git and Python 3 — no Node.js 🗺️ Then The GTD quest : a notes app, step by step Think of this page as level 0 : you set up your tools here, and the quest starts on the next page. No Node.js, no npm GTD does not use Node.js, npm or node_modules . You need only two small programs: Tool What it does Size esbuild Turns your TypeScript into one JavaScript file for the browser one file, ~10 MB Python 3 Serves the page on localhost while you work (already installed on Linux and macOS) — Nothing gets installed globally, there is no package.json , and your project folder stays tiny. 💡 Why a local server? Browsers refuse to load scripts from a file opened by double-click ( file://… ) in many cases. Any static server works; Python's is just already there. Step 1 — Get GTD 📦 git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/akrck02/gtd gtd-download mkdir -p my-app/src my-app/bin cp -r gtd-download/src my-app/src/gtd cp -r gtd-download/styles my-app/styles cd my-app GTD is not a package you install: it is a folder of source files that you copy into your project . You own them — you can read them, and even change them. The styles/ folder holds Bubble UI , the stylesheet that goes with GTD: nice buttons, colours, a dark theme and layout classes, in one 9 KB file. It is optional, but it makes your app look good from the first minute. Step 2 — Get esbuild 🔧 esbuild is a blender 🥤: you put in many .ts files — yours and GTD's — and get one .js file the browser can drink. On Linux (x86-64) the GTD repository already ships it: cp ../gtd-download/bin/esbuild bin/ On macOS, Windows or ARM , use esbuild's own installer, which downloads a single file: curl -fsSL https://esbuild.github.io/dl/v0.25.8 | sh mv esbuild bin/ Check it works: ./bin/esbuild --version # 0.25.8 Your project now looks like this: my-app/ ├── bin/ │ └── esbuild ← the builder ├── styles/ │ └── bubbleui-v3.0.0.css ← the looks └── src/ └── gtd/ ← GTD, one file per module ├── dom.ts ├── router.ts └── … Step 3 — Write the page 📄 Create index.html in my-app/ : <!doctype html> <html lang="en"> <head> <meta charset="utf-8"> <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> <title>My app</title> <link rel="stylesheet" href="./styles/bubbleui-v3.0.0.css"> <style> #app { padding: 2rem; gap: .5rem; } </style> </head> <body> <main id="app" class="box-column box-center"></main> <script type="module" src="./out/main.js"></script> </body> </html> <main id="app"> is the box where our pages will be drawn; Bubble's box-column box-center classes stack what we put in it and centre it. The <script> loads our code — it points to out/main.js , the file esbuild will build , not to the .ts file. Step 4 — Write the app ✍️ Create src/main.ts : import { uiComponent, setDomEvents } from "./gtd/dom.js" import { setRoute, showRoute } from "./gtd/router.js" import { BubbleUI } from "./gtd/bubble.js" // 1. Find the box where pages are drawn const app = document.getElementById("app") // 2. Describe the home page setRoute("/", async (_params, container) => { const title = uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "My first GTD app" }) const button = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: "Say hello", classes: [BubbleUI.Primary] }) setDomEvents(button, { click: () => location.hash = "/hello/world", }) container.append(title, button) }) // 3. Describe a second page; "$" means "any word here" setRoute("/hello/$", async ([name], container) => { const greeting = uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: `Hello, ${name}!` }) const back = uiComponent({ type: "a", text: "← Back", attributes: { href: "#/" } }) container.append(greeting, back) }) // 4. Draw the right page now, and every time the address changes const navigate = () => showRoute(location.hash.slice(1) || "/", app) window.addEventListener("hashchange", navigate) navigate() 💡 The imports end in .js even though the files are .ts . That is the standard way to write imports in TypeScript for the browser, and esbuild understands it. Step 5 — Build and run ▶️ ./bin/esbuild src/main.ts --bundle --format=esm --outfile=out/main.js python3 -m http.server 8000 The first command reads main.ts , follows every import , and writes one file, out/main.js . It takes a few milliseconds. Open http://localhost:8000 in your browser. You should see: The home page: a "My first GTD app" title and a "Say hello" button Click Say hello → the address ends in #/hello/world and the page greets you: The second page says "Hello, world!" with a link back Click ← Back → you are home again. Try typing #/hello/Ada in the address bar too. 🎉 That's it — you have a GTD app with routing. You are ready for the quest. Nothing on screen? Head to Troubleshooting . Making changes 🔁 Leave esbuild watching in a second terminal; it rebuilds every time you save: ./bin/esbuild src/main.ts --bundle --format=esm --outfile=out/main.js --watch Then just reload the browser after each change. Getting ready to publish 🌍 Add --minify to make the file small, and copy index.html and out/ to any static host (GitHub Pages, Netlify, your own server…): ./bin/esbuild src/main.ts --bundle --format=esm --minify --outfile=out/main.js Checking types (optional) 🔍 esbuild builds fast because it does not check types : a typo like contaner shows up in the browser, not in the terminal. Editors such as VS Code check types as you type. To check from the terminal too, the GTD repository has a script that downloads the native TypeScript compiler, again without Node: cp ../gtd-download/bin/install-ts.sh bin/ ./bin/install-ts.sh # downloads bin/tsgo once ./bin/tsgo --noEmit --strict false --target ES2022 --module ESNext --lib ES2022,DOM,DOM.Iterable src/main.ts What just happened? 🤔 How a GTD app is built: your TypeScript and GTD go through esbuild into one JavaScript file that index.html loads You wrote What it does uiComponent({...}) Creates a real HTML element — see Building the interface BubbleUI.Primary The name of Bubble's primary class: the blue, rounded button — see HTML tags and Bubble UI setDomEvents(button, { click }) Adds a click listener — same as addEventListener setRoute("/hello/$", view) Says which function draws which address — see Views and routing showRoute(path, app) Clears app and draws the matching page Next: choose your path 🧭 Path What you get 🗺️ The GTD quest (recommended) Build a notes app in 8 short levels, learning by doing 🧠 How GTD thinks Six ideas, five minutes, every other page becomes easier 📚 The guides Look up one thing when you need it ← All the documentation

guides/building-the-interface.title: Building the interface 🧱

sections.text: Reacting to clicks and other events
Changing an element after creating it

guides/building-the-interface.text:
Building the interface 🧱 Module: dom.ts · Depends on: nothing Everything you see on a web page is an element : a title, a button, an image. dom.ts helps you create elements and change them with less typing than plain JavaScript. In 30 seconds import { uiComponent } from "./gtd/dom.js" const hello = uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Hello!", classes: ["big"] }) document.body.appendChild(hello) Result on the page:

Hello!

Why not just document.createElement? You can! GTD only saves you the repetition. Compare: // plain JavaScript const link = document.createElement("a") link.textContent = "Docs" link.id = "docs-link" link.classList.add("nav", "active") link.setAttribute("href", "/docs") link.dataset.section = "help" // GTD const link = uiComponent({ type: "a", text: "Docs", id: "docs-link", classes: ["nav", "active"], attributes: { href: "/docs" }, data: { section: "help" }, }) Both give you exactly the same element. Creating an element uiComponent takes one object describing the element. Every field is optional. Field What it sets Example Default type The tag "button" "div" text What is inside (as HTML) "Save" empty id The id "save-button" none classes CSS classes ["primary", "big"] none attributes Any HTML attribute { href: "/home" } none styles Inline CSS, in camelCase { backgroundColor: "red" } none data data-* attributes { userId: "7" } → data-user-id="7" none selectable Can the user select its text? false true Text uiComponent({ type: "p", text: "A paragraph." }) uiComponent({ type: "p", text: "Some bold words." }) // HTML works ⚠️ Never put text typed by users into text . It is read as HTML, so a user could inject scripts into your page. For user text, set textContent after creating the element: const comment = uiComponent({ type: "p", classes: ["comment"] }) comment.textContent = userInput // always shown as plain text, safe Classes The usual way to style elements: write CSS in a stylesheet and add the class. uiComponent({ type: "button", text: "Delete", classes: ["button", "danger"] }) Attributes Anything you would write inside the HTML tag: uiComponent({ type: "img", attributes: { src: "./cat.png", alt: "A sleeping cat" } }) uiComponent({ type: "input", attributes: { type: "email", placeholder: "you@example.org" } }) uiComponent({ type: "a", text: "GTD", attributes: { href: "https://github.com/akrck02/gtd", target: "_blank" } }) Inline styles Good for quick experiments. Use the JavaScript names ( backgroundColor , not background-color ): uiComponent({ text: "Warning!", styles: { color: "white", backgroundColor: "crimson", padding: "8px" } }) Data attributes Store small pieces of information on an element, and read them later with dataset : const row = uiComponent({ type: "li", text: "Ada", data: { userId: "7" } }) row.dataset.userId // "7" Putting elements inside elements uiComponent gives you a normal element, so use the normal append : const card = uiComponent({ classes: ["card"] }) card.append( uiComponent({ type: "h2", text: "Ada Lovelace" }), uiComponent({ type: "p", text: "The first programmer." }), ) document.body.append(card) A good habit: write a small function per piece of interface. It is GTD's version of a "component": function userCard(name: string, bio: string): HTMLElement { const card = uiComponent({ classes: ["card"] }) card.append( uiComponent({ type: "h2", text: name }), uiComponent({ type: "p", text: bio }), ) return card } document.body.append(userCard("Ada", "First programmer"), userCard("Alan", "Codebreaker")) Reacting to clicks and other events import { setDomEvents } from "./gtd/dom.js" const button = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: "Click me" }) setDomEvents(button, { click: () => alert("Clicked!"), mouseenter: () => button.classList.add("hover"), mouseleave: () => button.classList.remove("hover"), }) Any DOM event name works: click , input , submit , keydown … To remove a listener later, you need the same function , so keep it in a variable: const onClick = () => console.log("clicked") setDomEvents(button, { click: onClick }) removeDomEvents(button, { click: onClick }) // works removeDomEvents(button, { click: () => console.log("clicked") }) // ❌ a different function, nothing happens Changing an element after creating it Each set… has a matching remove… . They all return the element, so you can chain them. To add To remove remove takes setDomClasses(el, ["active"]) removeDomClasses(el, ["active"]) class names setDomAttributes(el, { disabled: "" }) removeDomAttributes(el, ["disabled"]) attribute names setDomStyles(el, { color: "red" }) removeDomStyles(el, ["color"]) CSS names: "background-color" setDomDataset(el, { state: "open" }) removeDomDataset(el, ["state"]) dataset keys setDomEvents(el, { click: fn }) removeDomEvents(el, { click: fn }) the same functions // show a button as "loading" while saving setDomAttributes(button, { disabled: "" }) setDomClasses(button, ["loading"]) await save() removeDomAttributes(button, ["disabled"]) removeDomClasses(button, ["loading"]) If you pass undefined instead of the element or the values, nothing happens — no errors. Removing elements from the page import { removeDomById, removeAllDomBySelector } from "./gtd/dom.js" removeDomById("welcome-banner") // the element with id="welcome-banner" const count = removeAllDomBySelector(".toast") // every element with class "toast" console.log(`${count} toasts removed`) Or on an element you already have: element.remove() . Full example: a counter import { uiComponent, setDomEvents } from "./gtd/dom.js" let count = 0 const label = uiComponent({ type: "p", text: "Clicked 0 times" }) const button = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: "+1" }) setDomEvents(button, { click: () => { count++ label.textContent = `Clicked ${count} times` }, }) document.body.append(label, button) Common mistakes Symptom Cause Fix The element is created but not visible It was never added to the page parent.append(element) styles: { "background-color": … } does nothing Inline styles use camelCase backgroundColor removeDomStyles(el, ["backgroundColor"]) does nothing Removing uses CSS names "background-color" Text with < shows weird or breaks the layout text is HTML Use textContent for plain text ← All the documentation · Next: Views and routing →

guides/configuration.title: Configuration ⚙️

sections.text: Full example: a theme switch that remembers

guides/configuration.text: Configuration ⚙️ Module: configuration.ts · Depends on: nothing Store settings — the API address, the theme, the language — so they survive reloads . They are kept in the browser, on the user's device, as one JSON object. In 30 seconds import { setConfiguration, getConfiguration } from "./gtd/configuration.js" setConfiguration("theme", "dark") getConfiguration("theme") // "dark", even after closing the browser First step: name your configuration Open src/gtd/configuration.ts and change the id to your app's name: const configurationId: string = "my-notes-app" All your settings are saved together under that name. Two apps on the same address (for example both on localhost:8000 ) with the same id would share — and overwrite — their settings. Reading and writing Function What it does setConfiguration(key, value) Saves value under key getConfiguration(key) Returns the value, or undefined if it was never saved isConfigurationSet(key) true if key has a value isConfigurationActive(key) true only if the value is exactly true — handy for on/off options await loadConfiguration(path) Saves every key of a JSON file Values can be anything JSON can hold : text, numbers, booleans, lists and objects. They come back with the same type: setConfiguration("fontSize", 18) setConfiguration("favourites", ["1", "4"]) setConfiguration("animations", true) getConfiguration("fontSize") + 2 // 20 getConfiguration("favourites").length // 2 isConfigurationActive("animations") // true Defaults from a file Put the defaults in config.json , next to index.html : { "api": "https://example.org/api", "theme": "light", "animations": true } and load it when the app starts: await loadConfiguration("./config.json") Each key of the file is saved; keys that are only in the browser are kept. If a key is in both, the file wins . To keep what the user chose, load the file only the first time: if (!isConfigurationSet("api")) await loadConfiguration("./config.json") Full example: a theme switch that remembers Bubble UI has a dark theme built in: it turns on with data-theme="dark" on <html> . import { uiComponent, setDomEvents } from "./gtd/dom.js" import { getConfiguration, setConfiguration } from "./gtd/configuration.js" import { prefersDarkMode } from "./gtd/browser.js" import { BubbleUI } from "./gtd/bubble.js" function applyTheme(theme: string) { document.documentElement.dataset.theme = theme // Bubble UI: "light" or "dark" } // use the saved theme, or the system preference the first time let theme = getConfiguration("theme") ?? (prefersDarkMode() ? "dark" : "light") applyTheme(theme) const toggle = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: "Toggle theme", classes: [BubbleUI.Primary] }) setDomEvents(toggle, { click: () => { theme = "dark" == theme ? "light" : "dark" setConfiguration("theme", theme) applyTheme(theme) }, }) document.body.append(toggle) Light Dark The theme example in light mode The same page after pressing the button, in dark mode Good to know Settings are saved in localStorage : per site and per browser, so they don't travel between devices. Users can clear them at any time, so always have a default. Don't store passwords or other secrets there: any script on the page can read them. To see what's stored: developer tools → Application ( Storage in Firefox) → Local Storage → your configurationId . ← All the documentation · Next: Icons →

guides/icons.title: Icons ✨
guides/icons.text: Icons ✨ Module: icons.ts · Depends on: dom.ts Load a collection of SVG icons once, then draw any of them, at any size and colour, with one call. In 30 seconds import { loadIcons, getIcon } from "./gtd/icons.js" await loadIcons("ui", "./icons.json") document.body.append(getIcon("ui", "home")) The collection file A JSON file where each key is an icon name, and each value is what goes inside an <svg> tag, drawn on a 24 × 24 grid: { "home": "<path d=\"M10 20v-6h4v6h5v-8h3L12 3 2 12h3v8z\"/>", "close": "<path d=\"M19 6.4 17.6 5 12 10.6 6.4 5 5 6.4 10.6 12 5 17.6 6.4 19 12 13.4 17.6 19 19 17.6 13.4 12z\"/>" } 💡 Where do I get icons? Material Symbols and most icon sets use a 24 × 24 grid. Download an SVG, open it in a text editor, and copy what is between <svg …> and </svg> — usually one or more <path …/> . Remember to escape the quotes ( \" ) inside the JSON. Drawing icons getIcon(collection, name, size?, fill?) Argument Meaning Default collection The id you gave to loadIcons — name The key in the JSON file — size Width and height "24px" fill Colour "#222222" It returns a <div> (a flex box that centres the icon) with the <svg> inside, or undefined if the collection or the icon doesn't exist. getIcon("ui", "close", "16px", "crimson") getIcon("ui", "home", "2rem", "currentColor") 💡 Use "currentColor" as the colour: the icon then takes the text colour of its parent, so it follows your CSS, hover states and dark mode for free. An icon inside a button const button = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: " Home", classes: ["with-icon"] }) button.prepend(getIcon("ui", "home", "18px", "currentColor")) .with-icon { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 4px; } Several collections Give each collection its own id: await loadIcons("ui", "./icons/ui.json") await loadIcons("brands", "./icons/brands.json") getIcon("brands", "github") Common mistakes Symptom Cause Fix getIcon returns undefined loadIcons not awaited, or a typo in the id or name await loadIcons(...) first, check spelling Icon is invisible Same colour as the background Pass a fill , or "currentColor" Icon looks cut or tiny The SVG was not drawn on a 24 × 24 grid Use 24px icons, or edit viewBox in icons.ts JSON fails to load Unescaped quotes in the paths Write \" inside the strings ← All the documentation

guides/keyboard-shortcuts.title: Keyboard shortcuts ⌨️
guides/keyboard-shortcuts.text: Keyboard shortcuts ⌨️ Module: shortcuts.ts · Depends on: crypto.ts Let people use your app from the keyboard: Ctrl + S to save, Esc to close, / to search. In 30 seconds import Shortcuts, { KeyInteraction } from "./gtd/shortcuts.js" const keys = Shortcuts.register(document) Shortcuts.set(keys, { interaction: KeyInteraction.keyDown, key: "s", ctrlKey: true, preventDefault: true, // stop the browser's own "save page" callback: () => save(), }) Two steps Register where to listen: Shortcuts.register(target) returns an id. Use document for shortcuts that work everywhere, or an element for shortcuts that only work while it has the focus (an editor, a dialog). Set shortcuts on that id: Shortcuts.set(id, shortcut) . Setting the same combination again replaces it. const everywhere = Shortcuts.register(document) const inEditor = Shortcuts.register(editorElement) The shortcut object Field Required Meaning key ✅ The key, as the browser names it: "s" , "Enter" , "Escape" , "ArrowUp" , "/" … Letters ignore case interaction ✅ KeyInteraction.keyDown (when pressed, the usual one) or KeyInteraction.keyUp (when released) callback ✅ The function to run ctrlKey , shiftKey , altKey , metaKey Keys that must be held. metaKey is ⌘ on a Mac, ⊞ on Windows preventDefault Stop what the browser would do with that key ( Ctrl + S saving the page…) stopPropagation Stop other listeners from seeing the key repeatable Run again while the key is held down. Off by default omitEditableContent Do nothing while the user types in an input, a textarea or editable content 💡 The modifiers must match exactly : a shortcut for Ctrl + S does not run on Ctrl + Shift + S , and a shortcut for S alone does not run while Ctrl is held. Common recipes Close a dialog with Esc : Shortcuts.set(keys, { interaction: KeyInteraction.keyDown, key: "Escape", callback: closeDialog }) / to search, but not while typing: Shortcuts.set(keys, { interaction: KeyInteraction.keyDown, key: "/", omitEditableContent: true, // typing "/" in a text field must still type it preventDefault: true, callback: () => searchInput.focus(), }) Move through a list holding an arrow: Shortcuts.set(keys, { interaction: KeyInteraction.keyDown, key: "ArrowDown", repeatable: true, callback: selectNext }) Ctrl on Windows and Linux, ⌘ on a Mac: import { getOs } from "./gtd/browser.js" const mac = "MacOS" == getOs() Shortcuts.set(keys, { interaction: KeyInteraction.keyDown, key: "k", ctrlKey: !mac, metaKey: mac, preventDefault: true, callback: openSearch, }) Showing shortcuts to people Shortcuts nobody knows about are not used. Show them next to the action: const hint = uiComponent({ type: "kbd", text: mac ? "⌘ K" : "Ctrl K" }) searchButton.append(hint) ← All the documentation

guides/signals.title: Signals 📡

sections.text: Organising signals in a real app

guides/signals.text: Signals 📡 Module: signals.ts · Depends on: crypto.ts As an app grows, parts of it need to know when something happens elsewhere: when the user logs in, the header shows their name, the menu shows more options, the cart loads. A signal lets one part announce the event and any number of parts react , without importing each other. If you have used Godot, GTK or Qt, it is the same idea. Elsewhere it is called an event bus or the observer pattern . In 30 seconds import { setSignal, connectToSignal, emitSignal } from "./gtd/signals.js" const userLoggedIn = setSignal() // 1. create connectToSignal(userLoggedIn, async user => { // 2. listen console.log(`Welcome, ${user.name}!`) }) await emitSignal(userLoggedIn, { name: "Ada" }) // 3. announce // → Welcome, Ada! The login emits userLoggedIn; the header, the menu and the cart react, without knowing each other The three steps Step Function What it does Create setSignal() Returns a new, unique signal id (a string) Listen connectToSignal(id, handler) Calls handler(data) every time the signal is emitted Announce emitSignal(id, data) Calls every handler connected to id , with data , and waits for all of them Stop disconnectSignal(id) Removes every handler of id ; the signal can be connected again Organising signals in a real app Create all the signals in one file , so everyone imports the same ids: // src/events.ts import { setSignal } from "./gtd/signals.js" export const userLoggedIn = setSignal() export const cartChanged = setSignal() // src/header.ts import { connectToSignal } from "./gtd/signals.js" import { userLoggedIn } from "./events.js" connectToSignal(userLoggedIn, async user => { greeting.textContent = `Hi, ${user.name}` }) // src/cart.ts connectToSignal(userLoggedIn, async user => loadCart(user.id)) // src/login.ts — knows nothing about the header or the cart await emitSignal(userLoggedIn, { id: 7, name: "Ada" }) Adding a new reaction later means adding one connectToSignal , without touching login.ts . How it behaves Situation What happens Several handlers on one signal All run, in the order they were connected Emitting a signal that was never created Nothing Connecting to a signal that was never created An error in the console; the handler is ignored A handler that takes long (e.g. a request) await emitSignal(...) waits until every handler finished emitSignal(id) without data Handlers receive undefined Handlers start one after the other but run at the same time , so a slow one doesn't delay the others. But await emitSignal(...) waits for the slowest one: a handler that should not hold up the code that emits (an animation, a message that disappears later) should not await its slow part. Signals and pages A view that connects to a signal every time it is drawn would pile up handlers. Connect long-lived parts of the app (a header, a cart) once, at start. For a signal that belongs to one page, clear it before drawing the page again: setRoute("/chat", async (_, container) => { disconnectSignal(messageArrived) // forget the previous visit's handlers connectToSignal(messageArrived, async message => container.append(bubble(message))) }) Typing the data Handlers receive any . Give the data a type to get autocompletion: type User = { id: number, name: string } connectToSignal(userLoggedIn, async (user: User) => { user.name // autocompleted }) Full example: a cart badge import { uiComponent, setDomEvents } from "./gtd/dom.js" import { setSignal, connectToSignal, emitSignal } from "./gtd/signals.js" const cartChanged = setSignal() const cart: string[] = [] // the badge only listens const badge = uiComponent({ type: "span", text: "🛒 0" }) connectToSignal(cartChanged, async (items: string[]) => { badge.textContent = `🛒 ${items.length}` }) // the buttons only announce const products = ["Pencil", "Notebook"].map(name => { const button = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: `Add ${name}` }) setDomEvents(button, { click: () => { cart.push(name) emitSignal(cartChanged, cart) }, }) return button }) document.body.append(badge, ...products) ← All the documentation · Next: Translations →

guides/talking-to-a-server.title: Talking to a server 🌐

sections.text: Full example: load and show a list, with errors handled

guides/talking-to-a-server.text: Talking to a server 🌐 Module: http.ts · Depends on: nothing Apps load and save data: a list of products, a user profile, a new comment. http.ts sends those requests for you, with sensible defaults, using the browser's own fetch . In 30 seconds import { httpGet, httpPost } from "./gtd/http.js" // read const response = await httpGet({ url: "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1", parameters: {} }) const todo = await response.json() console.log(todo.title) // write await httpPost({ url: "/api/notes", parameters: { text: "Buy milk" } }) 💡 await means "wait for the answer before going on". Every function here is async , so put await in front of it, inside an async function or at the top of a module. The request object Every function takes one object: Field Required What it is Default url ✅ Where to send the request — parameters ✅ The data to send. Use {} when there is none — headers Extra headers, like a login token none contentType The data format "application/json" charset The text encoding "UTF-8" One function per HTTP method Function Use it to… Sends parameters ? httpGet read something ❌ — put values in the URL instead httpPost create something ✅ as JSON httpPut replace something ✅ as JSON httpPatch change part of something ✅ as JSON httpDelete delete something ✅ as JSON httpHead check something exists, without the body ✅ httpOptions ask what the server allows ✅ Sending values with GET GET has no body, so values go in the address: const search = encodeURIComponent("blue shoes") await httpGet({ url: `/api/products?search=${search}&page=2`, parameters: {} }) Reading the answer You get back a standard Response : const response = await httpGet({ url: "/api/me", parameters: {} }) response.ok // true for 200–299 response.status // 200, 404, 500… await response.json() // the body, parsed as JSON await response.text() // or as plain text ⚠️ A 404 or 500 is not an error for fetch : you still get a Response . Always check response.ok or the status. Errors ( throw ) only happen when there is no answer at all — no internet, wrong domain, blocked by CORS. Reacting to each status handleResponseStatus picks a function by status code, so your happy path and your error paths stay tidy: import { handleResponseStatus } from "./gtd/http.js" const response = await httpGet({ url: "/api/me", parameters: {} }) await handleResponseStatus( response, new Map([ [200, async res => showProfile(await res.json())], [401, async () => location.hash = "/login"], [404, async () => showMessage("User not found")], ]), async res => showMessage(`Something went wrong (${res.status})`), // everything else ) Without that last function, unknown statuses are written to the console. Logging in: adding headers const token = getConfiguration("token") await httpGet({ url: "/api/me", parameters: {}, headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` }, }) Uploading files Put the files in a FormData and send it as parameters . GTD sends it as multipart/form-data automatically. const input = uiComponent({ type: "input", attributes: { type: "file" } }) as HTMLInputElement setDomEvents(input, { change: async () => { const form = new FormData() form.append("picture", input.files[0]) form.append("title", "My cat") await httpPost({ url: "/api/upload", parameters: form }) }, }) Other formats The MimeType and TextEncoding enums list common values, so you don't have to remember them: import { httpPost, MimeType, TextEncoding } from "./gtd/http.js" await httpPost({ url: "/api/import", parameters: "name,age\nAda,36", contentType: MimeType.Csv, charset: TextEncoding.Utf8, }) Full example: load and show a list, with errors handled import { uiComponent } from "./gtd/dom.js" import { httpGet } from "./gtd/http.js" type Todo = { id: number, title: string, completed: boolean } async function showTodos(container: HTMLElement) { const status = uiComponent({ type: "p", text: "Loading…" }) container.append(status) try { const response = await httpGet({ url: "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos?_limit=5", parameters: {} }) if (!response.ok) { status.textContent = `The server answered ${response.status}` return } const todos: Todo[] = await response.json() status.remove() const list = uiComponent({ type: "ul" }) for (const todo of todos) { const item = uiComponent({ type: "li" }) item.textContent = `${todo.completed ? "✅" : "⬜"} ${todo.title}` list.append(item) } container.append(list) } catch { status.textContent = "Could not reach the server. Are you online?" } } showTodos(document.body) Common mistakes Symptom Cause Fix blocked by CORS policy The server doesn't allow your page's address Fix on the server ( Access-Control-Allow-Origin ) Data sent with httpGet never arrives GET ignores parameters Put values in the URL response.json() throws The answer is not JSON (often an HTML error page) Check response.ok first Got a Promise instead of data Missing await await response.json() ← All the documentation · Next: Signals →

guides/translations.title: Translations 🌍
guides/translations.text: Translations 🌍 Module: i18n.ts · Depends on: nothing i18n is short for internationalisation (an i, 18 letters, an n). This module lets your app show its texts in the user's language, keeping every text in JSON files instead of in the code. In 30 seconds Create resources/i18n/en/home.json : { "welcome": "Welcome!" } …and resources/i18n/es/home.json : { "welcome": "¡Bienvenido!" } Then: import { setCurrentLanguage, loadTextBundle, getText } from "./gtd/i18n.js" await setCurrentLanguage(navigator.language) // the browser's language, like "es-ES" await loadTextBundle("home") uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: getText("home", "welcome") }) // "¡Bienvenido!" in Spanish browsers Where the files go my-app/ ├── index.html └── resources/ └── i18n/ ├── en/ │ ├── home.json │ └── settings.json └── es/ ├── home.json └── settings.json One folder per language ( en , es …). One JSON file per bundle : a group of texts, usually one per page or feature. Each bundle has the same keys in every language. resources/ sits next to index.html (paths are relative to the page). To use another folder, change I18N_PATH at the top of i18n.ts . Splitting texts into bundles means each page only downloads the texts it needs. The three functions Function What it does await setCurrentLanguage(locale) Chooses the language: "es" , "es-ES" , navigator.language … await loadTextBundle(bundle) Downloads resources/i18n/<language>/<bundle>.json , once getText(bundle, key) Returns the text, or "" if it's not there Load bundles before drawing the views that use them, for example at the start of the view: setRoute("/settings", async (_, container) => { await loadTextBundle("settings") // does nothing if it is already loaded container.append(uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: getText("settings", "title") })) }) Letting the user change language await setCurrentLanguage("es", true) // true = download the loaded bundles again, in Spanish navigate() // draw the current page again with the new texts Remember the choice with Configuration , and use it at start: setConfiguration("lang", "es") // next time the app opens: await setCurrentLanguage(getConfiguration("lang") ?? navigator.language) Which languages are available Out of the box, English , Spanish , Galician and Catalan can be used. Any other locale falls back to English, with a warning in the console. To add a language, open src/gtd/i18n.ts and edit two places at the top: export const Languages = { English: { name: "english", main: "en", locales: ["en", "en-US", "en-GB"] }, Spanish: { name: "spanish", main: "es", locales: ["es", "es-ES"] }, Galician: { name: "galician", main: "gl", locales: ["gl", "gl-ES"] }, Catala: { name: "catala", main: "ca", locales: ["ca", "ca-ES"] }, French: { name: "french", main: "fr", locales: ["fr", "fr-FR", "fr-CA"] }, // ← new } const AVAILABLE_LANGUAGES = [ Languages.Spanish, Languages.English, Languages.Galician, Languages.Catala, Languages.French, // ← and enable it ] Field Meaning main The folder name under i18n/ locales Every code that should pick this language ( navigator.language gives values like "fr-CA" ) Then create resources/i18n/fr/ with the same bundles. To start in another language when the locale is unknown, change DEFAULT_LANGUAGE . Texts with values inside getText returns plain strings, so use placeholders and replace : { "greeting": "Hello, {name}!" } getText("home", "greeting").replace("{name}", user.name) When something is missing Situation What you get Bundle not loaded yet "" Key not in the bundle "" Bundle file missing or broken Skipped quietly; texts read "" Retry a flaky network loadTextBundle("home", false, 3) tries up to 3 times An empty text on screen almost always means a missing await loadTextBundle(...) or a typo in a key. Check the Network tab for a 404 on the JSON file. ← All the documentation · Next: Configuration →

guides/views-and-routing.title: Views and routing 🧭

sections.text: Option A — hash addresses (recommended to start)

guides/views-and-routing.text: Views and routing 🧭 Modules: router.ts , view.ts · Depend on: nothing Most apps have more than one page: a home, a profile, settings… The router decides which page to draw for the current address. In 30 seconds import { setRoute, showRoute } from "./gtd/router.js" setRoute("/", async (_params, container) => { container.textContent = "Home" }) setRoute("/about", async (_params, container) => { container.textContent = "About us" }) const app = document.getElementById("app") const navigate = () => showRoute(location.hash.slice(1) || "/", app) window.addEventListener("hashchange", navigate) navigate() Now #/ shows Home and #/about shows About us . How showRoute works: the address is matched against your routes, the matching view draws into the container Two words: view and route A view is a function that draws one page. It receives two things: params — values taken from the address (more on that below). container — the element to draw into. async function aboutView(params: string[], container: HTMLElement) { container.append(uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "About us" })) } Its type is viewHandler , from view.ts , if you want to write it down: import { viewHandler } from "./gtd/view.js" const aboutView: viewHandler = async (params, container) => { /* … */ } A route links an address to a view: setRoute("/about", aboutView) Addresses with values in them Put a $ where the address has a value that changes. The view receives the values, in order, in params : setRoute("/user/$", async ([userId], container) => { container.textContent = `Profile of user ${userId}` }) setRoute("/user/$/post/$", async ([userId, postId], container) => { container.textContent = `Post ${postId} by user ${userId}` }) Address View params /user/7 /user/$ ["7"] /user/7/post/42 /user/$/post/$ ["7", "42"] Values always arrive as strings . Convert them if you need numbers: Number(userId) . Home and "not found" "/" (or "" ) is the home page. You can also set it with setHomeRoute(view) . When no route matches, the not found view is shown. Set your own: import { setNotFoundRoute } from "./gtd/router.js" setNotFoundRoute(async (_params, container) => { container.append( uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Oops, this page does not exist" }), uiComponent({ type: "a", text: "Go home", attributes: { href: "#/" } }), ) }) Until you set them, GTD shows the words Home page. and Page not found. . Showing a page showRoute(path, container) : Empties container . Finds the route that matches path . Calls its view with the values and the container. To add a page below what the container already has, instead of replacing it, pass false : showRoute("/comments", container, false) . GTD does not listen to the address bar by itself — you choose how. There are two common ways. Option A — hash addresses (recommended to start) Addresses look like example.org/#/user/7 . They work on any host, GitHub Pages included, without configuring a server. const app = document.getElementById("app") const navigate = () => showRoute(location.hash.slice(1) || "/", app) window.addEventListener("hashchange", navigate) // when the address changes navigate() // and once at start Move to another page with a normal link, or from code: uiComponent({ type: "a", text: "Profile", attributes: { href: "#/user/7" } }) location.hash = "/user/7" Option B — clean addresses (/user/7) Uses the History API. Looks nicer, but the server must answer every address with index.html , or reloading a page gives a 404. function go(path: string) { history.pushState({}, "", path) showRoute(path, app) } window.addEventListener("popstate", () => showRoute(location.pathname, app)) // back / forward showRoute(location.pathname, app) // to navigate: go("/user/7") How a route is chosen You rarely need to think about this, but if two routes compete: Routes with more segments are tried first : for /docs/intro , /docs/$ wins over /docs . A trailing slash is ignored: "/settings/" is the same as "/settings" . $ matches one segment: anything except / . A route also matches longer addresses: /user/$ matches /user/7/anything . If you need both, register the longer one too. Full example: a small site import { uiComponent } from "./gtd/dom.js" import { setRoute, setNotFoundRoute, showRoute } from "./gtd/router.js" const app = document.getElementById("app") function menu(): HTMLElement { const nav = uiComponent({ type: "nav" }) nav.append( uiComponent({ type: "a", text: "Home", attributes: { href: "#/" } }), uiComponent({ type: "a", text: " · Products", attributes: { href: "#/products" } }), ) return nav } const products = ["Pencil", "Notebook", "Eraser"] setRoute("/", async (_, container) => { container.append(menu(), uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Welcome to the shop" })) }) setRoute("/products", async (_, container) => { container.append(menu(), uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Products" })) products.forEach((name, index) => { const item = uiComponent({ type: "p" }) item.append(uiComponent({ type: "a", text: name, attributes: { href: `#/products/${index}` } })) container.append(item) }) }) setRoute("/products/$", async ([index], container) => { container.append(menu(), uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: products[Number(index)] ?? "Unknown product" })) }) setNotFoundRoute(async (_, container) => { container.append(menu(), uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Not found" })) }) const navigate = () => showRoute(location.hash.slice(1) || "/", app) window.addEventListener("hashchange", navigate) navigate() Common mistakes Symptom Cause Fix Always "Page not found." Passing #/about instead of /about location.hash.slice(1) Clicking links does nothing No hashchange listener Add it, as above Pages pile up Drawing into document.body Draw into container Reload gives 404 with clean addresses Server doesn't serve index.html for every path Use hash addresses, or configure the server ← All the documentation · Next: Talking to a server →

overview.title: Welcome to GTD 👋

sections.text: Guides — one per thing you want to do
All the modules at a glance

overview.text: Welcome to GTD 👋 GTD ( Getting Things Done ) is a tiny TypeScript library for building web applications. It has one idea: the browser already knows how to build apps — GTD just makes it shorter to write. There is no virtual DOM, no special syntax, no compiler plugin and nothing to "learn instead of" JavaScript. A button made with GTD is a normal <button> . A request made with GTD is a normal fetch . If you know a little HTML and TypeScript, you already know most of GTD. import { uiComponent } from "./gtd/dom.js" const title = uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Hello, world!" }) document.body.appendChild(title) That is a complete GTD program. 🎉 No Node.js, no npm. You copy GTD's files into your project and build with esbuild , a single program. No node_modules , no configuration files. Is GTD for me? GTD is a good fit when you want: ✅ A small app, a tool, a dashboard or a personal site, without a big framework. ✅ To understand every line that runs in your page. ✅ To learn how the web platform works, while still writing less code. You may want something else when you need server-side rendering, a large component ecosystem or automatic re-rendering when data changes. Where to start New here? Follow these in order — the first two take about 10 minutes together. The GTD quest: 8 levels to build a notes app Step Page Time 1 Getting started — create a project and see it in the browser 5 min 2 How GTD thinks — the six ideas behind every module 5 min 3 The GTD quest — build a notes app in 8 short levels 45 min 🆘 Troubleshooting — blank page? errors in the console? look here — Guides — one per thing you want to do I want to… Read Module Put things on the screen Building the interface dom.ts Have several pages Views and routing router.ts , view.ts Load or send data to a server Talking to a server http.ts Let parts of my app react to each other Signals signals.ts Show my app in several languages Translations i18n.ts Remember user settings Configuration configuration.ts Show icons Icons icons.ts React to keyboard shortcuts Keyboard shortcuts shortcuts.ts Small helpers I want to… Read Module Know the screen size, dark mode or the device Browser browser.ts Style the page differently on phones Display display.ts Type text letter by letter, or fade things in Animations animations.ts Wait some milliseconds Time time.ts Make it look good (buttons, cards, dark theme) HTML tags and Bubble UI bubble.ts , html.ts Read parts of a URL or download a file Paths paths.ts Generate a random unique id Crypto crypto.ts Helping with GTD Page What it covers Contributing and testing Running the tests, code style, writing these docs All the modules at a glance Each module is one file. If you copy a module on its own, copy the modules it depends on too. Module Depends on What it gives you dom.ts — uiComponent and helpers to change elements view.ts — The viewHandler type router.ts view.ts setRoute , setHomeRoute , setNotFoundRoute , showRoute http.ts — httpGet , httpPost , httpPut , httpPatch , httpDelete , httpHead , httpOptions , handleResponseStatus signals.ts crypto.ts setSignal , connectToSignal , disconnectSignal , emitSignal i18n.ts — setCurrentLanguage , loadTextBundle , getText configuration.ts — loadConfiguration , setConfiguration , getConfiguration , isConfigurationSet , isConfigurationActive icons.ts dom.ts loadIcons , getIcon browser.ts — isSmallDevice , prefersDarkMode , isMobile , getOs … paths.ts — getUrlGetParameters , downloadFile … crypto.ts — uuidv4 display.ts browser.ts , configuration.ts , dom.ts checkDisplayType , isMobileDisplay (default) shortcuts.ts crypto.ts Shortcuts (default), KeyInteraction , Shortcut animations.ts html.ts , time.ts Animations (default) time.ts — sleep , sleepIf html.ts — Html (tag names) bubble.ts — BubbleUI (class names of styles/bubbleui-v3.0.0.css )

reference/animations.title: Animations 🎞️
reference/animations.text: Animations 🎞️ Module: animations.ts · Depends on: html.ts , time.ts Two small effects: text that types itself letter by letter, and elements that appear . In 30 seconds import Animations from "./gtd/animations.js" Animations.enabled = true // off by default const title = uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Hello, I'm GTD" }) document.body.append(title) await Animations.typing(title) // H… He… Hel… Hello, I'm GTD A title being typed letter by letter Turning animations on and off Animations.enabled is false until you set it. While it is false , every animation finishes at once, so the page simply shows its final state. Respect people who asked their system for less motion: import { prefersReducedMotion } from "./gtd/browser.js" Animations.enabled = !prefersReducedMotion() Animations.typing(element) Empties the text of the element and types it back at the speed of a fast typist. If the element has children, they are typed one after the other. It works on text elements: p , span , a , div , pre , code and h1 – h6 . Put the element on the page first , then await the animation: container.append(title, subtitle) await Animations.typing(title) await Animations.typing(subtitle) // starts when the title is done Animations.show(element) Adds the class show to the element, after letting the browser draw it once without it. Your CSS decides what "appearing" looks like: .card { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(8px); transition: all .3s; } .card.show { opacity: 1; transform: none; } const card = uiComponent({ classes: ["card"], text: "New message" }) container.append(card) await Animations.show(card) ⚠️ Without Animations.enabled = true the class is still added — just without the small pause — so make sure your CSS also works when the element appears at once. ← All the documentation

reference/browser.title: Browser 🖥️
reference/browser.text: Browser 🖥️ Module: browser.ts · Depends on: nothing Small questions about the device and the user's preferences, each answered by one function that returns true or false . In 30 seconds import { isSmallDevice, prefersDarkMode } from "./gtd/browser.js" if (isSmallDevice()) document.body.classList.add("mobile-layout") if (prefersDarkMode()) document.body.classList.add("dark") Screen size Function true when the window is Typical device isSmallDevice() 760px wide or less phone isMediumDevice() 760px to 1024px tablet, small laptop window isLargeDevice() wider than 1024px desktop They check the size when you call them . To react when the user resizes the window: window.addEventListener("resize", () => { document.body.classList.toggle("mobile-layout", isSmallDevice()) }) 💡 For pure styling, CSS media queries ( @media (max-width: 760px) { … } ) are simpler. Use these functions when the code must change, e.g. to draw a different menu. User preferences People set these in their operating system. Respecting them makes your app feel at home. Function true when the user… prefersDarkMode() uses a dark theme prefersLightMode() uses a light theme prefersReducedMotion() asked for fewer animations (motion can make some people dizzy) mediaQuery(query) matches any media query you write const animate = !prefersReducedMotion() const touchOnly = mediaQuery("(hover: none)") const printing = mediaQuery("print") Device and system Function Returns isMobile() Something truthy on Android, iPhone, iPad and other mobile browsers getOs() "Windows" , "MacOS" , "Linux" , "UNIX" , or undefined const shortcut = "MacOS" == getOs() ? "⌘ + S" : "Ctrl + S" uiComponent({ type: "small", text: `Save with ${shortcut}` }) These read the browser's user agent text, which can be changed or faked. Use them for small hints like the example above, not for important decisions. ← All the documentation

reference/crypto.title: Crypto 🔑
reference/crypto.text: Crypto 🔑 Module: crypto.ts · Depends on: nothing Create random, unique identifiers. In 30 seconds import { uuidv4 } from "./gtd/crypto.js" const id = uuidv4() // "3b241101-e2bb-4255-8caf-4136c566a962" When to use it Whenever you create something on the page that needs an id before the server gives it one: const note = { id: uuidv4(), text: "Buy milk" } Every call gives a new value; the chance of two being equal is so small you can ignore it. Good to know It follows the standard UUID version 4 format, which databases and servers understand. It uses the browser's secure random generator, so ids can't be guessed. Unlike the browser's crypto.randomUUID() , it also works on plain http:// addresses, for example on your local network while developing. ← All the documentation

reference/display.title: Display 📱
reference/display.text: Display 📱 Module: display.ts · Depends on: browser.ts , configuration.ts , dom.ts Decides once whether the app looks like a phone or a desktop app, and writes it on the page, so CSS and code can adapt. In 30 seconds import isMobileDisplay, { checkDisplayType } from "./gtd/display.js" checkDisplayType() window.addEventListener("resize", checkDisplayType) if (isMobileDisplay()) showBottomMenu() What checkDisplayType does It is mobile on a phone or tablet, or in a window up to 1024 pixels wide; otherwise desktop . Then it: Sets data-display on <html> : <html data-display="mobile"> or "desktop" . Saves "display" in the configuration , which isMobileDisplay() reads. Styling with it nav { display: flex; gap: 1rem; } [data-display="mobile"] nav { position: fixed; bottom: 0; justify-content: space-around; } Desktop Mobile A menu at the top on a wide window The same menu at the bottom on a phone 💡 Why not only CSS media queries? Because data-display also knows phones held sideways, which are wider than 1024 pixels sometimes, and because code can ask the same question with isMobileDisplay() , so CSS and TypeScript always agree. ← All the documentation

reference/paths.title: Paths 🔗
reference/paths.text: Paths 🔗 Module: paths.ts · Depends on: nothing Read pieces of a web address, and make the browser download a file. In 30 seconds import { getUrlGetParameters, downloadFile } from "./gtd/paths.js" getUrlGetParameters("https://shop.example.org/?search=shoes&page=2") // { search: "shoes", page: "2" } downloadFile("./reports/2026.pdf", "report.pdf") Query parameters (?key=value) const query = getUrlGetParameters(location.href) const page = Number(query["page"] ?? "1") Values come back exactly as written in the address. If they may contain spaces or symbols ( %20 …), decode them: decodeURIComponent(query["search"]) . Segments (/a/b/c) After a word — everything that follows a given segment: getUrlParametersByBreakPoint("https://example.org/search/user/1/page/2", "search") // ["user", "1", "page", "2"] getUrlParametersByBreakPoint("https://example.org/about", "search") // [] — "search" is not in the address From a position — splits on every / and keeps from that index: getUrlParametersByIndex("search/user/1/page/2", 2) // ["1", "page", "2"] With a full address, remember that https: , an empty piece and the domain count as the first three positions. 💡 Using the router ? It already gives your views the values of $ segments — you rarely need these functions for that. Downloading a file downloadFile(address, fileName) Works with files on your site and with data you create in the page: // a file from your site downloadFile("./docs/manual.pdf", "manual.pdf") // a file made on the fly const csv = "name,age\nAda,36\nAlan,41" const address = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([csv], { type: "text/csv" })) downloadFile(address, "people.csv") The browser only uses your fileName for files from your own site or created in the page; files from other sites keep their own name, or open in a new tab. ← All the documentation

reference/tags-and-styles.title: HTML tags and Bubble UI 🏷️

sections.text: What the stylesheet gives you for free

reference/tags-and-styles.text: HTML tags and Bubble UI 🏷️ Modules: html.ts , bubble.ts · Depend on: nothing · Stylesheet: styles/bubbleui-v3.0.0.css Two lists of names, so your editor can autocomplete them and typos become errors — and the stylesheet that makes GTD apps look good with almost no CSS. Bubble UI in 30 seconds Link the stylesheet in index.html : <link rel="stylesheet" href="./styles/bubbleui-v3.0.0.css"> and use its classes: import { BubbleUI } from "./gtd/bubble.js" const card = uiComponent({ classes: [BubbleUI.Surface1, BubbleUI.BoxColumn], styles: { padding: "1rem" } }) card.append( uiComponent({ type: "h2", text: "Welcome" }), uiComponent({ type: "button", text: "Start", classes: [BubbleUI.Primary] }), ) What the stylesheet gives you for free Without adding any class: A clean base: margins reset, the system font, a soft grey background. Buttons rounded like pills, that shrink a little when pressed. Inputs and text areas rounded, with a blue outline when focused. Links in the primary colour, without underline. Titles h1 – h6 with comfortable sizes and margins. A dark theme : set data-theme="dark" on <html> . document.documentElement.dataset.theme = prefersDarkMode() ? "dark" : "light" BubbleUI: the class names Layout — every box is a flexbox: Name Class Puts the children… BoxColumn / BoxColumnReverse box-column … top to bottom (or bottom to top) BoxRow / BoxRowReverse box-row … left to right (or right to left) BoxWrap box-wrap in lines that wrap BoxCenter box-center in the middle, both ways BoxXCenter / BoxXStart / BoxXEnd box-x-… centred, at the start or at the end, horizontally BoxYCenter / BoxYStart / BoxYEnd box-y-… centred, at the top or at the bottom, vertically BoxXBetween / BoxXAround box-x-between … spread out Colours — background and matching text colour, from the Material palette: Name Class Looks like Primary primary Blue, white text: the main button PrimaryContainer primary-container Light blue, rounded: a highlighted card Secondary , Tertiary (+ Container ) secondary … Calmer variants Error , ErrorContainer error … Red: errors and dangerous actions Surface1 , Surface2 , Surface3 surface-1 … Greys, rounded: cards and panels, darker each step Text : TextCenter , TextLeft , TextRight , TextTruncate (cut with … ), Bold , Italic . const toolbar = uiComponent({ type: Html.Nav, classes: [BubbleUI.BoxRow, BubbleUI.BoxXBetween, BubbleUI.BoxYCenter] }) const danger = uiComponent({ type: Html.Button, text: "Delete", classes: [BubbleUI.Error] }) 💡 Colours are CSS variables ( --primary-color , --surface-1 …). Change them in your own CSS to give your app its own palette: :root { --primary-color: #00796b; } Html: tag names import { Html } from "./gtd/html.js" uiComponent({ type: Html.Button, text: "Save" }) // instead of type: "button" uiComponent({ type: Html.Section }) It has the common tags ( Div , Span , P , A , H1 – H6 , Img , Ul , Li , Table …), form elements ( Input , Button , Select , Textarea , Label …) and SVG tags ( Svg , Path , Circle …). Writing "buton" by mistake gives you a broken element; writing Html.Buton does not compile. ← All the documentation

reference/time.title: Time ⏱️
reference/time.text: Time ⏱️ Module: time.ts · Depends on: nothing Wait some milliseconds inside an async function. In 30 seconds import { sleep, sleepIf } from "./gtd/time.js" status.textContent = "Saved ✓" await sleep(2000) // wait two seconds status.textContent = "" The functions Function What it does await sleep(ms) Waits ms milliseconds await sleepIf(ms, condition) Waits ms milliseconds only if condition is true ; otherwise continues at once sleepIf is handy for things that should be skippable: const animate = !prefersReducedMotion() for (const item of items) { list.append(item) await sleepIf(80, animate) // a little cascade, unless the user asked for less motion } 💡 sleep pauses only your function: the page keeps responding to clicks and scrolls while it waits. ← All the documentation

the-quest.title: The GTD quest
the-quest.text: The GTD quest Build a small app, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of GTD and ends with something new on your screen. The quest map: a road from START through 8 levels — Builder, Keeper, Messenger, Polyglot, Artist, Broadcaster, Shape-shifter and Speedrunner — to a final challenge, Notes Master We will build Notes : an app that lists your notes, opens them, speaks English and Spanish and remembers your choices. At the end, a small challenge: writing new notes. Every level has the same shape: the idea (explained with something from everyday life), the code , a checkpoint to know it works, and an optional bonus if you want a bit more. Go at your own pace — each level leaves you with a working app. Before you start You need the project from Getting started (5 minutes, if you haven't done it yet). Open two terminals in your project folder and leave these running the whole quest: # terminal 1 — rebuilds your app every time you save ./bin/esbuild src/main.ts --bundle --format=esm --outfile=out/main.js --watch # terminal 2 — serves it at http://localhost:8000 python3 -m http.server 8000 Now you only need to save and reload the browser after each change. Add this to the <style> in your index.html ; it makes the notes look like cards: .note { width: 100%; max-width: 420px; padding: 1rem 1.25rem; color: inherit; } This is where everything will live by the end: my-app/ ├── index.html ├── config.json ← level 2 ├── api/notes.json ← level 3 ├── resources/ │ ├── i18n/en/notes.json ← level 4 │ ├── i18n/es/notes.json ← level 4 │ └── icons.json ← level 5 └── src/ ├── gtd/ └── main.ts ← every level Level 1 · The Builder Mission Modules Time A home page, and one page per note dom , router 5 min The idea Think of LEGO . uiComponent gives you a brick — a title, a button, a card — and you click bricks into each other with append . The router is the receptionist of a building. You say "I'm going to /note/2 " , and they send you to the right room. That room is a view : a function that builds one page. How the router works: the address is matched against your routes, and the matching view draws into the container Build it Replace src/main.ts with: import { uiComponent } from "./gtd/dom.js" import { setRoute, showRoute } from "./gtd/router.js" const app = document.getElementById("app") // the home page setRoute("/", async (_, container) => { container.append(uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Notes" })) }) // one page per note: "$" catches the note number setRoute("/note/$", async ([id], container) => { container.append(uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: `Note ${id}` })) }) // draw the right page now, and every time the address changes const navigate = () => showRoute(location.hash.slice(1) || "/", app) window.addEventListener("hashchange", navigate) navigate() Checkpoint Open http://localhost:8000 : you see Notes . Now type #/note/3 at the end of the address: the page says Note 3 . Level 1: a page with the title "Notes" Bonus (optional): an "About" page Add a page at #/about that says who made the app. Achievement unlocked: Builder Learn more: Building the interface · Views and routing Level 2 · The Keeper Mission Modules Time Settings that survive closing the browser configuration 4 min The idea Your app forgets everything when you reload — like a goldfish. The configuration is a sticky note on the fridge : you write on it, close the tab, come back tomorrow… and it is still there. The first time, we fill it from a file with defaults. After that, the browser keeps it. Build it Create config.json next to index.html : { "api": "./api", "lang": "en" } Open src/gtd/configuration.ts and give your sticky note a name: const configurationId: string = "notes" At the top of src/main.ts , after the imports: import { loadConfiguration, getConfiguration } from "./gtd/configuration.js" // fill the sticky note only the first time, so your changes are kept if (undefined == getConfiguration("api")) await loadConfiguration("./config.json") Checkpoint Open the browser console ( F12 → Console ) and type localStorage.notes . You should see: '{"api":"./api","lang":"en"}' That is your sticky note. Reload the page: it is still there. Bonus (optional): a visit counter Count how many times the app was opened, and log it to the console. Achievement unlocked: Keeper Learn more: Configuration Level 3 · The Messenger Mission Modules Time Load your notes and show them as cards http , bubble 6 min The idea Asking a server for data is like ordering food delivery : You place the order → httpGet({ url }) You wait at home → await The courier hands you a closed box → a Response You open it → await response.json() Our "restaurant" is a JSON file in the project, so you need no real server. Build it Create api/notes.json : [ { "id": "1", "text": "Buy milk" }, { "id": "2", "text": "Call Ada" }, { "id": "3", "text": "Learn GTD" } ] Order the notes once, when the app starts: import { httpGet } from "./gtd/http.js" import { BubbleUI } from "./gtd/bubble.js" type Note = { id: string, text: string } const response = await httpGet({ url: `${getConfiguration("api")}/notes.json`, parameters: {} }) const notes: Note[] = await response.json() And show each one as a card . Bubble's surface-1 class gives it a soft background and round corners: setRoute("/", async (_, container) => { container.append(uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: "Notes" })) for (const note of notes) { container.append(uiComponent({ type: "a", text: note.text, classes: ["note", BubbleUI.Surface1], attributes: { href: `#/note/${note.id}` }, })) } }) setRoute("/note/$", async ([id], container) => { const note = notes.find(n => n.id == id) container.append(uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: note ? note.text : "No such note" })) }) Checkpoint Three cards on the home page. Click one: it opens. Level 3: the three notes shown as cards Bonus (optional): what if the restaurant is closed? Rename api/notes.json for a moment: the app breaks. Make it show a friendly message instead. Achievement unlocked: Messenger Learn more: Talking to a server · Bubble UI Level 4 · The Polyglot Mission Modules Time Your app in English and Spanish i18n 5 min The idea Think of subtitles . The film is the same; only the subtitle file changes. Your code says "show the title text" , and a JSON file per language says what that text is. Build it Create resources/i18n/en/notes.json : { "title": "Notes", "missing": "No such note", "switch": "Español" } …and resources/i18n/es/notes.json : { "title": "Notas", "missing": "No existe esa nota", "switch": "English" } Load the subtitles in the language of your sticky note: import { setCurrentLanguage, loadTextBundle, getText } from "./gtd/i18n.js" await setCurrentLanguage(getConfiguration("lang")) await loadTextBundle("notes") And replace the English words in your views with getText : container.append(uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: getText("notes", "title") })) container.append(uiComponent({ type: "h1", text: note ? note.text : getText("notes", "missing") })) Checkpoint In the console, switch the sticky note to Spanish and reload: localStorage.notes = '{"api":"./api","lang":"es"}' The title is now Notas . Bonus (optional): a third language GTD also knows Galician ( gl ) and Catalan ( ca ). Add one of them. Achievement unlocked: Polyglot Learn more: Translations Level 5 · The Artist Mission Modules Time A button, with an icon, that switches language icons , dom events 6 min The idea An icon collection is a sticker album : you load the album once, then stick any sticker anywhere, at any size and colour. A click event is a doorbell : you decide in advance what happens when someone rings it. Build it Create resources/icons.json with one sticker: { "translate": "<path d=\"M12.9 15.1 10.4 12.6v-.1A17 17 0 0 0 14 6h3V4h-7V2H8v2H1v2h11.2A16 16 0 0 1 9 11.4 16 16 0 0 1 6.7 8h-2a18 18 0 0 0 3 4.6L2.6 17.6 4 19l5-5 3.1 3.1zM18.5 10h-2L12 22h2l1.1-3h4.8l1.1 3h2zm-2.6 7 1.6-4.3 1.6 4.3z\"/>" } Load the album when the app starts: import { setConfiguration } from "./gtd/configuration.js" import { setDomEvents } from "./gtd/dom.js" import { loadIcons, getIcon } from "./gtd/icons.js" await loadIcons("app", "./resources/icons.json") And add the button at the end of the home page: const switchButton = uiComponent({ type: "button", text: getText("notes", "switch"), classes: [BubbleUI.Primary, BubbleUI.BoxYCenter], // blue, icon and text side by side styles: { gap: "6px" }, }) switchButton.prepend(getIcon("app", "translate", "16px", "currentColor")) // the doorbell: what happens on click setDomEvents(switchButton, { click: async () => { const lang = "es" == getConfiguration("lang") ? "en" : "es" setConfiguration("lang", lang) // write it on the sticky note await setCurrentLanguage(lang, true) // swap the subtitles navigate() // draw the page again }, }) container.append(switchButton) Checkpoint Press the button: the whole page changes language. Reload: it remembers. English Español The notes app in English, with an "Español" button The same app in Spanish, titled "Notas", with an "English" button Bonus (optional): a sticker on every card Add a second icon to icons.json and show it at the start of each note card. Achievement unlocked: Artist Learn more: Icons · Building the interface Level 6 · The Broadcaster Mission Modules Time Tell the rest of the app that the language changed signals 4 min The idea A signal is a radio station . The button broadcasts "language changed!" . Anyone tuned in reacts. The station doesn't know who is listening — and doesn't need to. This keeps your code tidy: tomorrow you can add another listener without touching the button. A signal: the login emits it, and the header, the menu and the cart react, without knowing each other Build it Create the station and a listener that writes in the browser tab's title: import { setSignal, connectToSignal, emitSignal } from "./gtd/signals.js" const languageChanged = setSignal() let changes = 0 connectToSignal(languageChanged, async lang => { changes++ document.title = `Notes (${lang}, ${changes} changes)` }) Broadcast from the button, after setCurrentLanguage : await emitSignal(languageChanged, lang) Checkpoint Look at the browser tab while you press the button: Notes (es, 1 changes) , Notes (en, 2 changes) … Bonus (optional): a second listener Tune a second listener to the same station: show a small message for two seconds. Achievement unlocked: Broadcaster Learn more: Signals Level 7 · The Shape-shifter Mission Modules Time Look good on a phone too display 3 min The idea You wear different clothes when it rains — same you, different outfit. checkDisplayType looks at the weather (the screen) and writes mobile or desktop on the page. Your CSS picks the outfit. Build it import { checkDisplayType } from "./gtd/display.js" checkDisplayType() // <html data-display="mobile"> or "desktop" window.addEventListener("resize", checkDisplayType) And the rainy-day outfit, in index.html 's <style> : [data-display="mobile"] body { font-size: 18px; } [data-display="mobile"] .note { max-width: none; } Checkpoint Open the developer tools, turn on the device toolbar (the phone icon, or Ctrl + Shift + M ) and pick a phone: bigger text, cards as wide as the screen. Level 7: the notes app on a phone, with wide cards Achievement unlocked: Shape-shifter Learn more: Display · Browser Level 8 · The Speedrunner Mission Modules Time Move around without the mouse shortcuts 3 min The idea You already use shortcuts every day: Ctrl + C , Ctrl + V . Speedrunners in games beat levels faster with them. Let's give your app some. Build it Press Ctrl + H anywhere to go h ome: import Shortcuts, { KeyInteraction } from "./gtd/shortcuts.js" const keys = Shortcuts.register(document) Shortcuts.set(keys, { interaction: KeyInteraction.keyDown, key: "h", ctrlKey: true, preventDefault: true, // don't open the browser's history callback: () => location.hash = "/", }) Checkpoint Open a note, press Ctrl + H : you are home. Bonus (optional): escape! Make Esc go home too. Achievement unlocked: Speedrunner Learn more: Keyboard shortcuts Final challenge · Notes Master Mission Modules Time Write new notes, and keep them after a reload everything you learned 10 min The challenge This time there is no step-by-step, but you already have every piece: You need to… You learned it in Draw a text box and a button Level 1 Keep the notes after a reload Level 2 Start from api/notes.json the first time Level 3 React to the button Level 5 Give each note a unique id uuidv4() from crypto.ts The goal: a text box and an + Add button on the home page. Type "Water the plants" , press + Add , and a new card appears. Reload: it is still there. Hint: keep the whole list on the sticky note — setConfiguration("notes", notes) — and read it back at start with getConfiguration("notes") . Try it on your own first, then compare with the solution. The final challenge: a text box and a plus button above the cards, with a new note "Water the plants" Rare achievement unlocked: Notes Master Well done All nine achievements: Builder, Keeper, Messenger, Polyglot, Artist, Broadcaster, Shape-shifter, Speedrunner and Notes Master You built a real app, and you can read every line of it. That is the GTD way. Ideas to keep going Idea Difficulty Hint Delete a note ⭐ A button on the note page, notes.splice(…) , setConfiguration Dark mode switch ⭐ document.documentElement.dataset.theme = "dark" — see Configuration Type the title letter by letter ⭐⭐ Animations Search your notes ⭐⭐ An input, notes.filter(…) , draw again on input events Save notes on a real server ⭐⭐⭐ httpPost — see Talking to a server Stuck at any point? See Troubleshooting . ← All the documentation

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting 🆘
troubleshooting.text: Troubleshooting 🆘 Something not working? Open the browser console first ( F12 , or right click → Inspect → Console ). The error there almost always points to one of these. Building ./bin/esbuild: Permission denied Make it executable: chmod +x bin/esbuild . ./bin/esbuild: cannot execute binary file (or Exec format error ) The esbuild in the GTD repository is for Linux x86-64. On macOS, Windows or ARM, download yours: curl -fsSL https://esbuild.github.io/dl/v0.25.8 | sh . On Windows, run it in Git Bash or WSL. Could not resolve "./gtd/dom.js" The path is wrong. Imports are relative to the file that has them: from src/main.ts , GTD's files are in ./gtd/ . Check that src/gtd/dom.ts exists. Top-level await is currently not supported with the "iife" output format Add --format=esm to the esbuild command, and keep type="module" on the <script> tag. My changes don't show up Is esbuild running with --watch , or did you run it again? Then reload without cache: Ctrl + Shift + R ( Cmd + Shift + R on a Mac). The page is blank GET http://localhost:8000/out/main.js 404 (Not Found) The app was not built yet, or went somewhere else. Run esbuild and check that out/main.js exists and matches the src of your <script> . Errors about modules or CORS, and the address starts with file:// You opened index.html by double-clicking it. Serve the folder instead: python3 -m http.server 8000 , then open http://localhost:8000 . Cannot use import statement outside a module The <script> tag needs type="module" . x is not defined or Cannot read properties of undefined , but it compiled esbuild does not check types, so typos reach the browser. Check the name in the error, or check types first: see Checking types in Getting started . Routing Every page shows "Page not found." Is setRoute called before showRoute ? Are you passing the path without the # ? Use location.hash.slice(1) . Is the route registered with a leading slash? setRoute("/about", …) , then go to #/about . Nothing happens when the address changes GTD does not watch the address bar for you. Add: window.addEventListener("hashchange", () => showRoute(location.hash.slice(1) || "/", app)) Pages pile up on top of each other Draw into the container your view receives, not into document.body . showRoute empties the container before each page. Translations, configuration, icons getText returns an empty string Did you await loadTextBundle("name") before calling getText ? Does ./resources/i18n/<language>/<name>.json exist? Check the Network tab for a 404. Is your language in AVAILABLE_LANGUAGES in i18n.ts ? See Translations . Settings of two apps mix up on localhost Both use the same configurationId . Set your app's name in configuration.ts . See Configuration . getIcon returns undefined Make sure you await loadIcons(...) first, and that the collection id and icon name are spelled the same as in the JSON file. Requests Access to fetch … has been blocked by CORS policy The server does not allow requests from your page's address. This is fixed on the server (it must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin ), not in GTD. While developing, serving your app and the API from the same address avoids it. My request fails but there's no error fetch — and so GTD — only throws on network failures. A 404 or 500 is a normal response: check response.ok or use handleResponseStatus . See Talking to a server . Still stuck? Open an issue at https://github.com/akrck02/gtd/issues with what you did, what you expected, and the console error. Small examples are the fastest to fix. ← All the documentation
